## The causes of the First World War

In the early twentieth century Europe was divided into two armed camps. The Triple Alliance linked Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy, and it was formed to protect its members from attack by France and Russia. In response, France, Russia and Britain drew closer together in the Triple Entente. Neither group was a formal military union at first, but the system meant that a quarrel between two countries could quickly drag in all the great powers.

Historians usually point to four main causes of the war:
- Militarism: the great powers built up huge armies and navies, and generals gained influence over governments.
- Alliances: the two blocs promised to support their members if one was attacked.
- Imperialism: rivalry over colonies in Africa and Asia caused friction between Britain, France and Germany.
- Nationalism: national pride and ethnic tensions, especially in the Balkans, threatened to break up Austria-Hungary.

Militarism was most obvious in the naval race between Britain and Germany. After Britain launched the revolutionary battleship HMS Dreadnought in 1906, Germany tried to match it ship for ship, and each side feared the other's growing fleet. Germany also had a large conscript army, and its leaders believed that Germany would have to fight both France and Russia at the same time.

Nationalism was strongest in the Balkans, where Serbia wanted to unite all the Slavs in the region. Austria-Hungary, which ruled many Slavs itself, saw Serbia as a threat. Russia presented itself as the protector of the Slavic peoples and so backed Serbia. This is why a local dispute in the Balkans became a European war.

## The outbreak of war

The spark came on 28 June 1914. Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb who belonged to a nationalist group. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and, after receiving a promise of support from Germany, sent Serbia an ultimatum in July. Serbia accepted most of its demands but not all, and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July.

Within a week the alliances had pulled in the other powers. Russia mobilised to defend Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and then on France, and Britain entered the war when German troops invaded neutral Belgium on 4 August 1914. Britain had promised in 1839 to protect Belgium, so it had a legal reason to act as well as a strategic one.

Germany's plan for a war on two fronts was the Schlieffen Plan. It aimed to defeat France quickly by marching through Belgium before Russia could get ready, and then to turn the whole army east. The plan failed. The Belgians resisted longer than expected, the British Expeditionary Force slowed the advance, and the German armies were stopped at the Battle of the Marne in September 1914.

## The course of the war

After the Marne both sides dug in, and the Western Front became a line of trenches stretching from the Channel to Switzerland. Trench warfare meant that attackers had to cross open ground called no man's land, swept by machine guns and artillery, and offensives produced terrible casualties for tiny gains. At the Battle of the Somme in 1916 the British suffered nearly 60,000 casualties on the first day alone.

The war became a total war, in which a country uses all of its resources and the whole population is involved. Factories were switched to making shells and rifles, men were conscripted in Britain from 1916, and women took over many jobs in industry and on the land. Governments used propaganda to keep up morale and rationing to share out scarce food. Civilians were attacked as well, by Zeppelin raids and by naval blockades.

In 1917 two events changed the balance of the war. Russia was swept by revolution and made peace with Germany, which allowed the Germans to move troops west. Germany's campaign of unrestricted submarine warfare then sank American ships, and the United States declared war in April 1917. The fresh American troops arrived in large numbers in 1918, just as the Germans launched their last great offensive.

The offensive failed, and the Allies pushed the German army back in the Hundred Days. Germany's allies collapsed one by one, there were mutinies and strikes at home, and the Kaiser abdicated. An armistice, which is an agreement to stop fighting, came into effect at 11 o'clock on 11 November 1918. About ten million soldiers had been killed.

## The peace settlement

The peace conference met in Paris in 1919, led by Britain, France and the United States. The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919, exactly five years after the assassination. It blamed Germany for the war under the war guilt clause, forced it to pay reparations, took away its colonies and part of its land, and limited its army to 100,000 men.

Many Germans hated the treaty and called it a Diktat, because they had no say in it. Others thought it was too harsh for a lasting peace, while the French thought it was too lenient. Historians still argue about how far the treaty helped to cause the Second World War.

President Woodrow Wilson wanted a fairer peace based on his Fourteen Points, which included self-determination for nations. His most important idea was the League of Nations, an international organisation set up in 1920 to keep peace by collective security. It was weakened from the start because the United States Senate refused to join, and Germany and Russia were not allowed in at first. The League could not stop aggression by powerful countries in the 1930s.
